name: Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate
route: IV infusion every 8 weeks for 4 doses, in a nuclear medicine unit
status: FDA-approved in 2018 for somatostatin receptor-positive GEP-NETs; extended to children 12 and older in 2024
mechanism: A somatostatin look-alike that carries radioactive lutetium-177 into neuroendocrine tumor cells, where its radiation damages their DNA

article.summary: Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate (Lutathera) is a radioactive peptide drug that targets neuroendocrine tumors. FDA-approved in 2018, it is given as four IV infusions eight weeks apart.
article.takeaway: Lutathera is a form of radioligand therapy: a targeting peptide that delivers radiation straight to tumor cells that carry somatostatin receptors. In the NETTER-1 trial for advanced midgut tumors, **65% of patients were progression-free at 20 months**, versus 11% on high-dose octreotide alone.[^1] Given first-line for higher-grade tumors in NETTER-2, it lengthened median progression-free survival from 8.5 to **22.8 months**.[^2] It can lower blood counts and, rarely, lead to bone marrow cancers years later.[^3]
glance: Approved January 2018; ages 12 and older since 2024
Four IV infusions, 8 weeks apart, with kidney-protecting amino acids
Two randomized phase 3 trials (NETTER-1 and NETTER-2)

blocks.text: Most well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors are studded with somatostatin receptors. Lutathera uses dotatate, a peptide modeled on the hormone somatostatin, to find those receptors. Attached to it is lutetium-177, a radioactive metal that gives off short-range beta radiation.

Once the drug binds, it is pulled inside the tumor cell, and the radiation breaks DNA in that cell and its close neighbors. Because the beta particles travel only a few millimeters, most of the dose stays in the tumor, although the kidneys and bone marrow also receive some. The same peptide labeled with gallium-68 is used for [PET scans](/peptides/ga-68-dotatate) to confirm a tumor is a good target first.

Lutathera is approved for adults and children 12 and older with GEP-NETs that show somatostatin receptors on imaging, including tumors of the foregut, midgut and hindgut.[^3] It is typically used when tumors are advanced or cannot be removed with surgery, either after progression on a somatostatin drug or, for some higher-grade tumors, as a first treatment.

rows: Progression-free at 20 months: 65.2% vs 10.8% on high-dose octreotide; tumors shrank in 18% vs 3%[^1]
Same trial, about 6 years of follow-up
Median survival 48.0 vs 36.3 months, a difference that was not statistically significant[^4]
226 adults with newly diagnosed grade 2-3 GEP-NETs

blocks.text: The investigators judged the 11.7-month difference in median survival to be clinically relevant, even though it missed statistical significance. No new safety signals appeared during long-term follow-up.[^4]

Each dose is 7.4 GBq (200 mCi), infused into a vein every 8 weeks for four doses. An amino acid solution runs from 30 minutes before until at least 3 hours after each infusion to reduce radiation to the kidneys, and anti-nausea medicine is given first. Long-acting octreotide is given after each dose and continued between and after treatments.[^3]
Patients are radioactive for a short time afterward and receive instructions on limiting close contact, especially with children and pregnant people, and on hygiene for the days that follow.

items: **Common:** nausea and vomiting (partly from the amino acid infusion), fatigue, low blood counts, and changes in liver tests
**Bone marrow:** blood counts are checked before each dose; doses may be delayed or reduced

**Secondary blood cancers:** myelodysplastic syndrome developed in 2 of 111 treated patients in NETTER-1;[^4] across studies it appeared a median of 29 months after treatment, and acute leukemia a median of 55 months[^3]
**Kidneys and liver:** function is monitored throughout treatment
**Hormonal crisis:** flushing, diarrhea or low blood pressure can flare as tumors release hormones
**Pregnancy and fertility:** can harm a fetus and may cause infertility; effective contraception is needed

evidence.label: Approved: two randomized phase 3 trials
evidence.text: Large progression-free survival benefits were shown in two randomized phase 3 trials, one after somatostatin drug failure and one as a first treatment.[^1][^2] An overall survival advantage has not been statistically proven.

faq.q: How do doctors know whether Lutathera will work?
faq.a: A somatostatin receptor PET scan, such as [Ga-68 dotatate](/peptides/ga-68-dotatate), shows whether the tumors take up this type of peptide. Strong uptake is required before treatment.
No. It is targeted radiation delivered by a peptide, often called peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). Side effects differ from chemotherapy, though blood counts can still drop.

faq.q: Will I be radioactive after treatment?
faq.a: Yes, for a limited time. The treatment team gives instructions on distance, sleeping arrangements and bathroom hygiene for the days after each dose.
